title: Prefix Caching Technical Deep Dive - Meridian Dynamics
summary: SE-led deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Meridian's multi-tenant LLM service. Covered cache keys, hit rate targets, eviction policies, multi-tenant safety (isolation, HMAC signing), metrics to track, and implications for VPC/on-prem deployments and quantized runtimes. Action items and next steps agreed: run benchmark, share cache design doc, produce pilot scope and SLOs.
topics: Interaction with KV cache and batching
action_items: Carlos (Redwood) - Share prefix caching design doc and sample key hashing function - due 2026-03-10
Raj (Meridian) - Provide anonymized sample prompt distribution and tenant request rates - due 2026-03-08
Maya (Redwood AE) - Send pilot pricing and SOW draft - due 2026-03-12
next_steps: Run 48h benchmark with 3 tenant profiles and share results
Redwood to propose per-tenant namespace approach and HMAC signing for cached entries
Schedule follow-up POC scoping call after benchmark (w/in 2 weeks)
transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-03-03 09:00 PST | Duration: 57m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Ivy (Redwood SA), Jenna (Meridian PM), Raj (Meridian Infra), Sofia (Meridian Security), Liam (Meridian ML)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro, this is a technical deep dive on prefix caching strategy. Carlos will lead.
[00:18] Carlos: Hi all, yep I'll run through our typical patterns, hit rates we've seen, common pitfalls. Please jump in anytime.
[00:28] Jenna: Quick context, our stack is multi-tenant inference, about 120 active tenants, mix of chat and LLM completion, tail latency SLO 200ms p50 for interactive flows, p95 450ms. Cost is big - we want caching to reduce token compute for repeated prompts.
[00:46] Carlos: Got it. Two driving goals: reduce per-token compute for repeat prefixes, and avoid correctness/ security issues across tenants. We'll talk cache keys, namespace isolation, TTLs, eviction, and how this interacts with KV cache and batching.
[01:05] Raj: Quick Q on infra: we're on a VPC-hosted private deployment right now with dedicated nodes, some on-prem testing planned. Any caching assumptions that break in air-gapped infra?
[01:18] Ivy: Good note - on-prem or VPC means you control KMS/keys so we recommend HMAC signing of cache keys using customer-managed key, we can provide patterns that work offline.
[01:30] Sofia: From security we worry about cache poisoning and cross-tenant leakage. How do you ensure a tenant can't retrieve another tenant's cached prefix?
[01:42] Carlos: We namespace by tenant id and include tenant id in the hash, plus we recommend signing the key bytes. So a key shape might be: HMAC(K_customer, tenant_id || model_id || prompt_fingerprint || config_hash). If you keep the tenant id private and sign with tenant KMS, cross-tenant reads impossible unless key compromised.
[02:10] Liam: Is there overhead for that HMAC on every request? We're latency sensitive.
[02:18] Carlos: HMAC check is tiny - microseconds. More impactful is cache lookup latency and potential serialization if you use remote KV store. We typically keep a small in-process LRU for ultra-fast hits and back it with a regional redis or RocksDB for warm entries.
[02:42] Jenna: Can you run through what you mean by 'prompt_fingerprint' - how do you handle near-duplicates or templated prompts?
[02:52] Carlos: Good question. Fingerprint is usually a normalized prefix: whitespace normalization, placeholder normalization for user vars, and sometimes a small tokenizer-based sketch like the first N tokens hashed. For templated prompts we recommend replacing user-specific slots with stable placeholders before hashing. That increases hit rate without leaking PII.
[03:15] Raj: We have a lot of short prefixes identical across tenants (e.g., standard system prompts). If many tenants share the same normalized prefix, do you recommend a global cache versus per-tenant copy?
[03:28] Carlos: Tradeoff. Global shared entries save memory and improve global hit rate, but you must ensure outputs are safe to reuse - if you use tenant-specific instruction sets or context, don't share. Our pattern: categorize prefixes into public (safe to share) and private. Public prefixes can be cached globally with a shared key that omits tenant id; private prefixes include tenant id. We also allow a flag per-route to force private namespace.
[03:58] Sofia: How do you classify public vs private automatically? That's a risk if misclassified.
[04:06] Ivy: We don't fully automate - we provide heuristics and a review workflow. E.g., system prompts from product teams flagged as public, any prompt with user data is private. For POC, manual classification is fine. For scale, you can integrate a policy evaluation step to mark keys.
[04:25] [small crosstalk]
[04:33] Carlos: Next, hit rate targets. In our experience with chat workloads, good prefix normalization yields 30-60% prefix cache hit rate for stable system messages and common developer prompts. For heavy templating apps it's lower unless you normalize aggressively.
[04:55] Jenna: We ran a quick sample and saw about 12% identical prefix occurrences across requests - is that low?
[05:03] Carlos: It's not unusual. With normalization and canonicalization you can often push that to 25-40% depending on app. For Meridian's workload we might aim for 25% hit rate in phase 1.
[05:16] Liam: What's the latency delta on hit vs miss?
[05:20] Carlos: Depends on where cache lives - in-process LRU hits are sub-ms, regional redis 2-6ms added, remote cold fetch can be 20-80ms depending on bandwidth and model. But most important is token compute saved: a hit can avoid decoding the prefix tokens and reduce KV cache growth.
[05:44] Raj: You mentioned KV cache - how does prefix caching interact with model KV cache and batching?
[05:51] Carlos: Two layers: prefix/prompt cache stores precomputed partial generation state we can reuse, e.g., cached key/value tensors for the prefix. The runtime then attaches that to the request so the model doesn't recompute those tokens. This reduces per-token computation and can lower latency for the first output tokens. Batching still works - we can merge requests at the decoder stage but we need to align sequence lengths; prefix reuse reduces KV size so batching is more efficient.
[06:26] Liam: For quantized models, does prefix reuse hold the same? Any caveats with int8 or int4 kernel paths?
[06:35] Carlos: Good catch. Quantization changes kernel selection and sometimes storage format for KV tensors. We store cached KV in the same quantized format used at runtime to avoid expensive dequant/quant cycles. But that means cache entries are per-model-variant (e.g., fp16 vs int8). So include model variant/quantization tag in the config_hash.
[06:57] Jenna: How do you handle cache invalidation on model rollouts?
[07:02] Carlos: We version keys with model_id and model_hash; when rolling out a new model you effectively start with a different namespace. We also support coordinated invalidation: a migration job can rehydrate hot prefixes for the new model in a background pass.
[07:18] Sofia: For audit/compliance, do you log cache reads? We need to prove no cross-tenant access and have audit trails.
[07:27] Ivy: Yes, per-read logging with tenant id, key fingerprint, hit/miss, latency is standard. Logs can be routed to your SIEM. We can redact prompt contents in logs and only include fingerprints and hashes.
[07:43] Raj: Eviction strategy - LRU vs TTL vs cost-based?
[07:48] Carlos: We usually combine: keep a small in-process LRU for hottest entries, remote tier with LFU-friendly eviction or TTLs. Also maintain a cost metric: estimated token savings per entry, and evict low-benefit items when memory pressure is high. For multi-tenant fairness, enforce per-tenant memory quotas - prevents noisy neighbor.
[08:14] Jenna: Per-tenant quotas add complexity. How do you set them? Dynamic based on commits?
[08:19] Maya: Sales note - for Dedicated/Private customers we can expose quota knobs and offer reserved cache capacity.
[08:25] Carlos: For setting quotas, start with proportionate allocation by recent traffic and a reserve pool. Monitor cache hit marginal utility and auto-adjust.
[08:36] [timestamp noise]
[08:42] Liam: Does Redwood support multi-tenant safe global caching out of box or is it config work?
[08:48] Carlos: Out of the box we default to tenant-isolated keys. Global shared caches are opt-in with gating flags and classification. For Private deployments you can choose to enable global caches in config.
[09:00] Jenna: Any concerns about using shared caches in regulated environments?
[09:04] Sofia: Yes, compliance teams will push for isolation.
[09:07] Ivy: Correct, for regulated workloads we recommend strict tenant isolation and customer-managed KMS.
[09:12] Raj: Benchmarks - what should we run to validate?
[09:16] Carlos: 48-hour replay of representative traffic with three tenant profiles: low, medium, high concurrency. Measure: prefix cache hit rate, miss latency, end-to-end p95/p50, token cost reduction, KV cache size, and false-positive reuse incidents (if any). We'll instrument and supply a benchmarking harness.
[09:37] Jenna: Can you share an example key composition?
[09:40] Carlos: Example key: version|tenant_flag|HMAC_prefix, where HMAC_prefix = Base64(HMAC(K, tenant_id || model_id || prompt_fingerprint || quant_tag || route_config_hash)). If public, tenant_flag=public and tenant_id omitted.
[09:57] Raj: If we sign keys with our KMS then Redwood cannot read raw prompts for cache; is that supported?
[10:03] Ivy: Yes, customer-managed KMS means Redwood sees only the signed key; we can't derive prompt contents. For on-prem air-gapped, signing is local. We also support blind-hash patterns where Redwood stores opaque keys and acts as a KV layer without prompt visibility.
[10:18] Sofia: How about replay attacks - someone could take a signed key and replay to get different outputs?
[10:26] Carlos: We include route_config_hash and timestamp or TTL so keys have bounded validity. Also optionally include a nonce or request-specific salt to prevent reuse across different contexts. For deterministic caching we need stability, so usually TTL+basis config works. For high security, short TTLs and on-request signing is used.
[10:50] Liam: Impact on model quality - any risk of stale prefix leading to unexpected outputs?
[10:56] Carlos: If the model changes semantics or prompt templates change, yes. That's why model/version and config hashes are part of keys. Also we recommend continuous evals: run a small eval suite against cached vs live prefixes to detect regressions.
[11:14] Jenna: Okay, practical: can we start with tenant-isolated caching and a small shared public bucket for known safe prefixes?
[11:22] Carlos: Yes that's a common phased approach.
[11:25] Maya: I'll capture that as the recommended pilot.
[11:28] Raj: One last thing - metrics dashboards. What metrics should we add to our console?
[11:33] Carlos: Per-tenant: prefix hit rate, miss latency, avg saved tokens per hit, eviction rate, cache memory usage, and number of sign failures. Global: aggregate hit rate, top cached prefixes, hot-tenant list, and cost savings estimate.
[11:52] Jenna: We'll need a CSV or spreadsheet with the benchmark results schema so our infra team can run it.
[11:58] Carlos: We'll send a harness link and a template.
[12:02] [wrap up] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send design doc, bench harness, proposed pilot SOW and pricing. Meridian to send sample prompts/traffic and confirm 3 tenant profiles. Follow-up call in ~2 weeks to review benchmark. Any objections?
[12:20] Sofia: No objections from security as long as HMAC + per-tenant isolation in phase 1.
[12:25] Jenna: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:30] Carlos: Thanks, bye.

Notes: transcript contains occasional misrecognitions (e.g., 'KV cash' in some lines), some punctuation issues consistent with ASR. How to balance global shared cache vs per-tenant copies?
What metrics to instrument for pilot?
